It told Treasury and Commerce to evaluate “legal considerations… including any need for legislation,” and said the order must be carried out “consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.”
That is the core constraint: the Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse. A president cannot invent a new pot of money, move existing appropriations into a new investment vehicle, or create a new government investment entity with its own mandate just by executive order.Goal by goalMaximize stewardship of national wealth
Talking about it requires no Congress. Building a standalone fund that invests federal assets for long-term return does. Legal analyses after the order said capitalizing a new fund by “repurposing” existing assets would likely violate appropriations law or amount to double-counting. A proper fund needs either new appropriations or a dedicated funding stream Congress writes into statute.
Promote fiscal sustainability and reduce the tax burden
Reducing taxes is almost entirely Congress’s job. A fund that generates enough returns to replace tax revenue or pay down debt would first have to be large and profitable. The U.S. runs large deficits, so there is no surplus to seed it with. Creating that vehicle and authorizing how its returns are used requires legislation.

Long-term economic security for future generations
This is the classic purpose of funds like Alaska’s or Norway’s. Those exist because a legislature created them and dedicated a revenue stream. A federal version with durable governance (so a later president cannot raid it) would need a statute, not just an executive order.

U.S. economic and strategic leadership abroad
This is the piece he can do partly without a new fund. The administration has already taken equity stakes in semiconductors, rare earths, and other firms using existing authorities and money Congress had already appropriated (CHIPS Act funds, Defense Production Act, etc.). 2026 Election Security Report Card

 1. Election Record IntegritySite’s 2020 claim: Voter rolls, histories, ballot images, and related records were missing, altered, or showed more ballots than voters (examples they cite: Michigan, Pennsylvania, Fulton County, GA).

mitigation: DOJ sent demand letters to all 50 states + D.C. warning of criminal liability for keeping noncitizens on rolls; sued ~30 states for voter-roll access; obtained a North Carolina consent order covering ~100,000 voters lacking HAVA identifiers; prosecutions of some noncitizen voters (examples named: Denis Bouchard, several Florida cases, Haoxiang Gao). Homeland-security grants were conditioned on voter-to-ballot reconciliation and documentary citizenship checks.
Site’s caveat: 21 consecutive litigation losses or stays as of August 2026; states resisted data access. Effectiveness rated low on this vector.

2. Electronic Voting System IntegritySite’s 2020 claim: Machines (especially Dominion) had high-severity vulnerabilities, reused passwords, disabled firewalls, cellular modems, and tools that could alter tallies without logs; 319 classified-severity issues suppressed.
 mitigation: Seizure and analysis of Dominion equipment in Puerto Rico by Mojave Research; declassification of CIA/NSA/FBI material on Venezuelan and other alleged capabilities; DHS briefings to states on cyber issues.

3. Election Results Certification IntegritySite’s 2020 claim: Certifications proceeded despite missing records, statutory problems, and pressure.
 mitigation: EO 14248 (March 2025) revoked Biden-era EO 14019 and emphasized verification, documentary proof of citizenship, and hand-count/pre-certification audits. Grant conditions required hand-count auditing and reconciliation. EO 14399 (March 2026) directed federal “State Citizenship Lists” and USPS ballot-tracking rules.

4. Judicial MalfeasanceSite’s 2020 claim: Courts timed rulings, limited discovery, and blocked forensic access so challenges failed.
 mitigation: The report card treats later litigation losses and stays themselves as continuation of this vector rather than listing new executive “fixes.” Special attorneys and grand juries were appointed, but the site notes courts still issued stays on key rules.


 5.  ControlSite’s 2020 claim: Vulnerability data was classified, witnesses suppressed, and narratives controlled.
 mitigation: Declassification of 11 archives totaling 562 pages (269 pages released July 16, 2026) covering voting-system vulnerabilities, China’s alleged acquisition of ~200 million voter records, Michigan files, and noncitizen analyses. President’s July 16 primetime address announced this. Dismantling of the Global Engagement Center and related information-operations offices.

  mitigation: Rescissions Act of 2025 cancelled ~$8.97 billion (including Corporation for Public Broadcasting funding). FTO designations and Treasury orders against cartels; 62% drop cited in certain human-smuggling financial reports.

  • Trump mentioned Thune’s name after he said Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) “will go down as the greatest Speaker of the House in the history of our country.” He then added that Thune was “here” before asking where he was, prompting boos from the audience.
  • “No, no. John is working hard. He’s got great opposition. He’s got great opposition from the Democrat –– Schumer and these guys, they’re terrible. Great opposition,” he continued, referring to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). “He’s working very hard. He’s going to have great success. You watch.”
  • The president added that Senate Republicans will in general have “great, great success.”

Source: thehill.com
